mechanism: Ginkgotoxin (4'-O-methylpyridoxine) in ginkgo seeds and some leaf preparations can lower seizure threshold. Additionally, ginkgo may induce CYP2C19, potentially reducing valproate levels.
management: Use ginkgo with caution in patients with seizure history. Seizure monitoring is recommended. High-quality, standardized ginkgo leaf extract with controlled ginkgotoxin levels is preferable.

mechanism: Both omega-3 fatty acids and ginkgo biloba (via ginkgolides inhibiting PAF) independently inhibit platelet aggregation, producing additive antiplatelet/bleeding risk.
management: Monitor for signs of bruising or prolonged bleeding, especially before surgery. Consider separating or reducing doses.

mechanism: Both omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin E suppress platelet aggregation via separate pathways (membrane phospholipid remodeling and inhibition of platelet thromboxane synthesis), producing additive antiplatelet effects.
management: Monitor for signs of easy bruising or bleeding. Consider keeping supplemental vitamin E below high-dose ranges (≤400 IU/day, roughly 180-268 mg alpha-tocopherol depending on form) when taking fish oil.

mechanism: Ginkgo constituents can affect platelet function. A retrospective observational study found associations between ginkgo drug interactions and bleeding, including aspirin and clopidogrel combinations. These associations do not establish causation or a quantified risk for every patient.
management: Avoid combining ginkgo with antiplatelet drugs unless your prescriber specifically recommends it. Tell your surgical team about ginkgo before any procedure and follow their instructions on when to stop it. Do not stop a prescribed antiplatelet on your own.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis and GI mucosal protection. Omega-3s additionally inhibit platelet aggregation. Combined, GI bleeding risk and systemic antiplatelet effect are additive.
management: Use caution combining high-dose fish oil (>2 g/day) with NSAIDs. Take NSAIDs with food to protect GI lining. Monitor for GI symptoms. Discuss with doctor if using regularly.

mechanism: Garlic supplements may affect platelet function. Combining them with NSAIDs may increase bleeding risk; the retained monographs do not establish a 600 mg safe-below threshold.
management: Discuss garlic supplements with your prescriber if you use NSAIDs regularly. Watch for unusual bruising or gastrointestinal bleeding.

mechanism: Ginkgo inhibits PAF and platelet aggregation. NSAIDs inhibit COX-mediated thromboxane synthesis. The combined antiplatelet effect increases GI and systemic bleeding risk.
management: Avoid ginkgo with regular NSAID use. Watch for GI bleeding, unusual bruising. Inform prescriber of all supplements.

mechanism: Ginkgo has antiplatelet activity; SSRIs also impair platelet function by depleting serotonin in platelets. Combined, bleeding risk is increased. Additionally, ginkgo may have serotonin-modulating properties that could interact with SSRIs.
management: Avoid high-dose ginkgo with SSRIs. If used for cognitive support, discuss with your doctor. Monitor for unusual bruising.

mechanism: Garlic supplements may affect platelet function and increase bleeding risk with warfarin. The cited monographs do not establish a 600 mg safe-below threshold or clinically demonstrated CYP2C9 inhibition.
management: Talk to your warfarin prescriber before starting, stopping or changing garlic supplements. Ask whether INR checks are needed and report unusual bruising or bleeding.

mechanism: Ginkgo can affect platelet function and may increase bleeding risk with warfarin. Serious bleeding has been reported, but controlled and observational findings are mixed; a uniform or quantified increase in risk is not established.
management: Avoid combining ginkgo with warfarin. If ginkgo is being used, inform prescriber immediately. Watch for signs of bleeding (unusual bruising, prolonged cuts, blood in urine/stool).

mechanism: Fish oil can have antiplatelet effects at high doses and might affect INR with warfarin. NIH ODS notes that most research at 3–6 g/day does not significantly affect anticoagulant status and reviews have not found clinically significant bleeding overall. A case report describes bleeding after a fall with 6 g/day omega-3 plus aspirin and warfarin; it does not establish a warning threshold.
management: Tell your prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting, stopping, or changing fish oil while taking warfarin. Periodic INR monitoring may be appropriate, and watch for unusual bruising or bleeding. Do not change warfarin on your own.
